                 I. INTRODUCTION AND PERSONAL INFORMATION

Q.      Please state your name and address.
A.      My name is Ronald L. Boultinghouse. My wife, Deborah A. Boultinghouse, and I are
        joint owners and full-time year-round residents of the real property located at 2322
        County Road 205, Lampasas, Texas 76550. The property is in Burnet County, Texas. My
        telephone number is 512-751-8317. My email address is ronboultinghouse@gmail.com.

Q.      Are you an intervenor in this proceeding?
A.      Yes. I am a pro se intervenor in PUC Docket No. 59475 and SOAH Docket No. 473-26-
        16349. I am a directly affected landowner within the meaning of 16 TAC § 22.103 and 16
        TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) because the proposed Segment H3 alignment of the Bell County
        East Switch to Big Hill Substation 765-kV transmission line places the proposed
        centerline approximately 389.83 feet from the habitable structure at 2322 County Road
        205 in which my wife and I have continuously resided since approximately 1983, and
        crosses County Road 205 - our sole practical access road - directly at our driveway
        frontage. I filed my Request to Intervene and Landowner Statement with the Public
        Utility Commission of Texas Interchange on April 27,2026.

Q.      Please state your familiarity with the property.
A.      I have continuously owned, occupied, improved, and worked this property for more than
        forty-three years. I know the property at the level of detail at which only the owner-
        occupant of a working ranch homeplace can know land - every fence line, every gate,
        every gully, every spot where the limestone surfaces, every place the wet-weather creek
        runs after a heavy rain, the depth at which the well draws, the line of sight from the
        kitchen window, the spots where the cattle congregate in the heat, and every foot of
        County Road 205 from my driveway to the low-water crossing 1.5 miles east. I am not a
        witness reading this property off of a map. I am the owner, operator, and 365-day-per-
        year occupant of it.

Q.      Are you testifying on your own behalf?
A.      Yes. I am testifying on my own behalf and on behalf of the property at 2322 CR 205 and
        the household that resides on it. I am not appearing for any company, association, or
        other entity. I speak only from my own personal knowledge of my home, my land, my
        well, my access road, my livestock operation, and my community.

Q.      Have you ever testified before the Public Utility Commission of Texas?
A.      No. I have never previously testified before the Public Utility Commission of Texas, the
        State Office of Administrative Hearings, or any other administrative tribunal. I am a

                                 II. PURPOSE OF TESTIMONY

Q.      What is the purpose of your testimony?
A.      The purpose of this testimony is to place before the Commission and the Administrative
        Law Judge the parcel-level facts that compel the categorical rej ection of Segment H3 of
        the proposed Bell County East to Big Hill 765-kV transmission line, and any end-to-end
        route that incorporates Segment H3. Specifically, this testimony: (1) establishes the
        property-specific facts at 2322 CR 205 that demonstrate the H3 alignment fails every
        applicable factor of PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101 (b)(3)(B); (2) documents
        that the Applicants approached the H3 routing without the parcel-level diligence the
        routing rules require; (3) demonstrates that the Applicants failed to use the existing
        compatible rights-of-way available in the corridor; (4) demonstrates that the H3
        alignment violates the prudent-avoidance policy embedded in the Commission's own
        rules; and (5) makes the record on which the Commission must reject H3 outright, not
        modify it, condition it, or accept generic mitigation commitments in lieu of rej ection.

Q.      What is your position on Segment H3?
A.      My position is categorical: Segment H3 cannot be approved. No micro-alignment of H3
        can be approved. No conditioned, mitigated, or modified version of H3 can be approved.
        No end-to-end route that incorporates Segment H3 can be approved. The defects in the
        H3 routing are not cured by additional studies, supplemental mitigation, or post-hoc
        commitments. The defects are structural - they exist in the way the Applicants
        identified, drew, and selected the H3 alignment in the first instance - and they require
        the Commission to reject H3 and direct the Applicants to a route that does not include it.

Q.      Are you asking the Commission to require additional studies, additional metrics, or
        additional analysis of H3?
A.      No. I am not asking the Commission to require additional studies, additional metrics, or
        additional analysis of H3. I am asking the Commission to recognize, on the record now
        before it, that the H3 routing was not approached properly in the first instance - that the
        parcel-level facts at 2322 CR 205 and along the H3 corridor were either not known, not
        weighed, or not given the weight the routing rules require - and to rej ect H3 on that
        record without remand for further work on this alignment. The remedy for an alignment
        selected in violation of PURA § 37.056(c) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) is rejection of
        the alignment, not iterative refinement of it.

     III. SUMMARY OF POSITION - CATEGORICAL REJECTION OF H3

Q.      Please summarize the grounds on which Segment H3 must be rejected.
A.      Segment H3 must be rej ected on the following independent and cumulative grounds, each
        of which is developed in this testimony:
        First - Prudent-avoidance failure under 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B). The proposed H3
        centerline is approximately 389.83 feet from our habitable residence, by aerial
        measurement on the Applicants' own mapping. That distance is more than 110 feet inside
        the 500-foot prudent-avoidance setback envelope the Commission applies under its own
        rule. The prudent-avoidance failure is compounded by the fact that a member of our
        household has a documented heart arrhythmia and may require an implanted pacemaker.
        A 765-kV centerline less than 400 feet from a continuously occupied family residence, in
        a household with documented implanted-cardiac-device risk, is not prudent avoidance
        under any defensible reading of the rule.
        Second - Failure to use existing compatible rights-of-way under 16 TAC §
        25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii). Existing electric-transmission and rural-distribution infrastructure is
        already present in the immediate area surrounding the H3 study reach. The H3 alignment
        as drawn does not parallel that existing compatible right-of-way to the extent reasonably
        available; instead, it stacks a second extra-high-voltage corridor onto a community that
        already carries one, placing the new centerline within 400 feet of habitable structures
        rather than within the existing utility corridor.
        Third - Environmental-integrity failure under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(D) and 16 TAC §
        25.101(b)(3)(B)(iv). The H3 alignment at our property crosses karst-prone limestone
        bedrock of the Edwards Plateau / Lampasas Cut Plain transition zone, regulated by the
        Central Texas Groundwater Conservation District; crosses or runs immediately adjacent
        to a wet-weather creek; and is in a watershed where CR 205 itself includes a low-water
        crossing approximately 1.5 miles downstream that is impassable during heavy-rain
        events. Construction of a 765-kV corridor on this terrain - with the foundation-drilling,
        blasting, vibration, and clearing that voltage class requires - is not consistent with the
        environmental-integrity factor on any parcel-level analysis of this terrain.
        Fourth - Community-values failure under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A). The H3 alignment
        concentrates the burden of an industrial extra-high-voltage corridor on a small number of
        multi-generational rural homeplaces along CR 205 and within the Lake Victor
        community, including our property, which has been continuously owned and occupied by
        the same family since approximately 1983. The concentration of an extra-high-voltage
        corridor on this small set of identifiable rural families fails the community-values factor
        on its face; the Applicants have made no parcel-level record that supports it; and the
        failure is structural to the H3 alignment, not curable by adjustment.

        Fifth - Historical and aesthetic-values failure under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(C). Warner
        Cemetery, a historic community burial ground, and the Lake Victor community, a
        recognized historical rural community in Burnet County, are both within approximately
        one mile of our property. The H3 alignment would replace, not moderate, the rural visual
        setting of both. The Applicants did not conduct parcel-level Texas Historical Commission
        cultural-resource screening for the H3 corridor before designating it.

        Sixth - Sole-access road crossed at the driveway. County Road 205 is the only practical
        access to our home, our well, our workshop, and our cattle operation. The H3 corridor
        crosses CR 205 directly adj acent to our driveway frontage. The Applicants have not
        addressed, at the parcel level, the construction-phase access interference, the storm-phase
        access interference, the emergency-response interference, or the operational-phase access
        risk this crossing creates for the household at 2322 CR 205.
        Seventh - Sole water supply exposed to construction risk. Our entire household and
        livestock water supply comes from a single on-site well, approximately 483 feet deep,
        producing approximately 10 gallons per minute. The Applicants have not addressed, at
        the parcel level, the risk to that well from foundation drilling, blasting, or vibratory
        installation on karst-prone limestone within construction-influence distance.
        Eighth - Local-service failure under PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(E). The H3 alignment is part
        of a 765-kV bulk-power transmission project intended to move power across the ERCOT
        footprint pursuant to HB 5066 and the ERCOT Comparison Plan. It is not coupled to
        local distribution. Our retail electric service is provided by Pedernales Electric
        Cooperative, and the H3 alignment does not include a step-down substation that would
        serve the Lake Victor / CR 205 community. The H3 alignment does not improve electric
        service at our meter, does not reduce our electric cost, and is not an alignment that serves
        the affected community in any local-service sense recognized by PURA §
        37.056(c)(4)(E).
        Ninth - Constraint-stacking that is dispositive on its own. The H3 alignment at our
        property stacks prudent-avoidance failure (residence within 500 feet), sole-access-road
        crossing (CR 205 at the driveway), sole-water-supply exposure (the 483-foot well), karst-
        prone limestone bedrock, wet-weather creek crossing, and cumulative-burden
        concentration on a small number of multi-generational families. Any one of those factors
        is a meaningful regulatory flag under the Commission's rules. The concentration of all of
        them on the same parcel and the same access road is, on the record before the
        Commission, dispositive against approval.
        Each of these grounds is independently sufficient to reject Segment H3. The combined
        record compels rejection.

                    IV. PROPERTY DESCRIPTION AND LOCATION

Q.      Please describe your property.
A.      The property consists of approximately 25 acres located at 2322 County Road 205,
        Lampasas, Texas 76550, in Burnet County. My wife and I acquired the property in or
        about 1983 and have continuously owned, occupied, and worked it since acquisition. The
        land is gently rolling rural acreage in the Lampasas Cut Plain / Edwards Plateau transition
        zone of Central Texas, with native pasture, scattered live oak and cedar canopy, and
        visible limestone bedrock underlying the entire parcel. The improvements on the property
        include: (a) our primary residence - a full-time, year-round, 24-hour-per-day, 365-day-
        per-year habitable structure within the meaning of 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B); (b) a
        workshop building used continuously for ranch maintenance and equipment storage; (c)
        barns and sheds; (d) perimeter fencing and pasture cross-fencing; (e) corrals and working
        pens used for livestock handling; and (f) a single on-site water well, drilled to
        approximately 483 feet, producing approximately 10 gallons per minute. We have
        continuously operated a small working cattle operation on the property since acquisition.
        The original boundary survey of the property was performed at acquisition in or about
        1982 to 1983 and the survey records are on file at our bank.

Q.      Where is your property located relative to the proposed Segment H3 alignment?
A.      Our property is bisected by the proposed Segment H3 alignment along its western side.
        The proposed H3 centerline runs north-to-south on the western portion of our parcel and
        crosses County Road 205 directly at our driveway frontage. Aerial measurement on the
        Applicants' own mapping places the proposed centerline at approximately 389.83 feet
        from our residence - well within the 500-foot prudent-avoidance setback envelope that
        16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) applies to habitable structures along proposed transmission
        centerlines. The 200-foot easement that would be acquired for H3 would impose
        permanent vegetation-management, access, and use restrictions across the western
        portion of the parcel and across the developed footprint of the homeplace, including the
        area around the workshop, the area around the well, and the corrals and working pens.

Q.      How is access to the property obtained?
A.      Access to the property is by a single driveway off County Road 205. CR 205 is a county-
        maintained rural road and is the only practical access to our home, our well, our
        workshop, and our cattle. There is no secondary or alternate access route - no rear
        driveway, no easement to a parallel road, and no alternate-route gate. CR 205 itself
        includes a low-water crossing approximately 1.5 miles east of our driveway that becomes
        impassable during heavy-rain events. When that low-water crossing is over the road, our
        practical route in and out of the property is materially constrained. The proposed H3

               V. LAND USE AND MULTI-GENERATIONAL HISTORY

Q.      Please describe the history of your property and your association with it.
A.      My wife and I acquired the property in or about 1983 and have continuously owned,
        occupied, and worked it for more than forty-three years. We raised our family on this
        land. We built up the working cattle operation on this land. We drilled the well that
        serves the house and the livestock. We added the workshop, the barns, and the sheds over
        the decades as the family and the operation grew. We have buried more than one good
        dog under the oaks on this property. Our son may build his own residence on this same
        property in the future. The property is, in every functional sense recognized by Texas
        rural-property practice, a multi-generational family homeplace. PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A)
        directs the Commission to consider exactly that kind of community value, and PURA §
        37.051(c-1) and (c-2) direct the Commission to prefer routing that preserves the
        established use of multi-generational rural land.

Q.      How is the property currently used?
A.      The property is currently used as our full-time, year-round residence and as a working
        ranch homeplace. The principal uses are: (a) primary residence - 24-hour-per-day, 365-
        day-per-year habitable occupancy by my wife and me; (b) working cattle operation -
        small-scale commercial cow-calf operation continuously operated since acquisition; (c)
        pasture management - including rotational grazing, brush control, and fence
        maintenance consistent with Central Texas rural-range practice; (d) livestock handling -
        corrals and working pens used routinely for sorting, veterinary work, calving
        management, and seasonal herd operations; (e) workshop and equipment storage - used
        continuously for routine ranch maintenance; (f) groundwater use - single on-site well at
        approximately 483 feet, supplying all household and livestock water; (g) seasonal family
        activity - including lawful hunting in season; and (h) future improvement contemplation
        - including the possibility that our son will build a residence on the property. The
        property is not vacant, undeveloped, transitional, or speculative - it is in active, daily,
        continuous use that has been uninterrupted for more than four decades.

        working pens, and well - meaning the developed footprint of the homeplace sits inside
        the very band that 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B) directs the utility to avoid; (3) construction-

     VI. COMMUNITY VALUES AND AESTHETICS - PURA § 37.056(C)(4)(A)

Q.      What community values are relevant to the Commission's evaluation of Segment
        H3?
A.      PURA § 37.056(c)(4)(A) requires the Commission to consider the community values of
        the area through which a transmission line is proposed to pass. The community values
        along the H3 corridor in the vicinity of CR 205 and the Lake Victor area are well
        documented: (a) the rural working-ranch character of this portion of Burnet County,
        anchored on small and mid-sized family homeplaces; (b) the multi-generational
        continuity of ownership - including our forty-three-year ownership of 2322 CR 205 and
        the comparable long-term ownerships of the neighboring families along CR 205 and
        Warner Lake Victor Cemetery Road; (c) the Hill Country / Lampasas Cut Plain
        transitional viewshed, with intact pasture, mature tree canopy, and limestone-belt skyline
        largely uninterrupted by large overhead linear infrastructure; (d) the Lake Victor
        community itself, a recognized historical rural community in Burnet County with a long-
        standing settlement pattern and identity; and (e) Warner Cemetery, a historic community
        burial ground within approximately one mile of our property. With the exception of
        existing transmission and rural distribution infrastructure already present in the area
        surrounding the H3 study reach, the H3 corridor passes through a landscape that does not
        currently host large overhead linear infrastructure at the 765-kV scale.

Q.      How would the H3 alignment affect those community values?
A.      The H3 alignment would: (a) introduce a permanent, large-scale industrial corridor -
        765-kV class structures, on the order of 130 to 198 feet tall depending on configuration,
        at approximately 1,000- to 1,300-foot tower spacings - across a landscape that does not
        presently host comparable infrastructure at that scale; (b) place that industrial corridor in
        immediate visual and physical proximity to our residence (approximately 389.83 feet to
        the centerline) and to the residences of other long-tenured rural families along CR 205
        and the Lake Victor / Warner Cemetery community; (c) replace, rather than moderate, the
        rural viewshed from the residence, the workshop yard, the driveway on CR 205, the
        corrals, and the area around the well; (d) impose those visual and physical changes for the
        operating life of the line, typically fifty years or more; and (e) concentrate that
        cumulative burden on a small number of identifiable rural families, which is the precise
        community-values failure that the moderation-of-impact analysis under PURA §
        37.056(c) was written to prevent. The Application as filed does not adequately weigh
        those changes at the parcel level; it cannot, because the parcel-level facts of 2322 CR 205
        and the surrounding properties do not appear, with the requisite detail, in the Application.

Q.      How important are views and visual character to your property?

A.      Views and visual character are not a luxury on a rural Central Texas homeplace; they are
        a defining feature of the property and a substantive component of its value. From our
        residence and from every daily working area of the property - the porch, the kitchen
        window, the workshop yard, the driveway, the corrals, the pastures - the view consists

        25.101(b)(3)(B) and consistently applied in CCN proceedings before this Commission -
        that requires transmission-line applicants and the Commission to consider the proximity
        of habitable structures to proposed transmission centerlines and to prefer alignments that
        avoid, where reasonably possible, placing habitable structures within a 500-foot setback
        envelope from the centerline. The Commission's obligation is not merely to count
        habitable structures inside the envelope; it is to evaluate whether the Applicants have
        demonstrated that reasonable alternative alignments do not exist that would reduce the
        count of affected habitable structures, and to weigh that record against the other statutory
        factors. Where, as here, the Applicants have not demonstrated that reasonable alternative
        alignments are unavailable, the prudent-avoidance policy of the rule is not satisfied.

     XV. FAILURE TO USE EXISTING COMPATIBLE RIGHTS-OF-WAY - 16
                         TAC § 25.101(B)(3)(B)(II)

Q.      What does the Commission's rule require regarding existing compatible rights-of-
        way?
A.      PURA § 37.051(c-1) and (c-2) and 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii) establish a routing
        preference for paralleling existing compatible rights-of-way - including existing
        transmission corridors, pipeline corridors, roadways, and railroad corridors - where
        reasonably available. The preference is not a license to label any nearby corridor
        'compatible' and proceed; it is a substantive routing factor that requires the Applicants to
        demonstrate, on the record, that they have used existing compatible ROW to the extent
        reasonably available, and to justify deviation from existing compatible ROW where they
        have not.

Q.      Does the H3 alignment as drawn use existing compatible rights-of-way to the extent
        reasonably available?
A.      No. Existing electric transmission and rural distribution infrastructure is already present
        in the immediate area surrounding the H3 study reach. The H3 alignment as drawn does
        not parallel that existing utility ROW to the extent reasonably available; instead, it routes
        the new 765-kV corridor through a working multi-generational homeplace and across the
        only practical access road of that homeplace, placing the new centerline approximately
        389.83 feet from a habitable structure rather than within the existing utility corridor. That
        is the precise routing failure 16 TAC § 25.101(b)(3)(B)(ii) was written to identify, and it
        is independent of every other defect in the H3 alignment described in this testimony.

Q.      Why does this failure require rejection rather than modification of H3?
A.      The use-of-existing-compatible-ROW preference is a routing-level factor, not a
        centerline-level factor. The defect is not that the H3 centerline could be moved a few tens
        of feet to better parallel existing ROW; the defect is that the H3 corridor was identified,
        drawn, and selected without the parallel-routing analysis the rule requires. Once that
        analysis is performed on the parcel-level record now before the Commission, the result is
        that H3 is the wrong corridor - not that H3 is the right corridor with a different
        centerline. The remedy for an alignment selected in violation of the use-of-existing-
        compatible-ROW preference is rejection of the alignment, with end-to-end route
        selection turning to alternatives that do not include H3.
